paragraphs.heading: The study of life
paragraphs.text: Biology is the science of life and of living things. It is a broad natural science, made of many fields and shared principles that explain how life is built, how it works, grows and spreads, where it came from and how it evolves. Biologists look at life at several levels, from molecules and cells up to whole organisms, populations and ecosystems.

paragraphs.heading: Five big themes
paragraphs.text: Five themes sit at the heart of the subject. The cell is the basic unit of life. Genes and heredity are how traits get passed on. Evolution drives the variety of living things. Life also depends on transforming energy, and on homeostasis, which means keeping conditions inside the body stable.

paragraphs.heading: Branches and methods
paragraphs.text: The subject splits into branches such as ecology, physiology, molecular biology, developmental biology, systematics and evolutionary biology. Each branch studies living things through observation, experiments and mathematical models. Biologists also sort organisms, from single-celled bacteria and archaea to plants, fungi and animals, by the traits they share and how they are related through evolution.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word joins the Greek bíos, meaning life, with logia, meaning study of. It shows up in the title of a 1766 volume by Michael Christoph Hanow. In its modern sense, it seems to have been brought in separately by several people: Thomas Beddoes (1799), Karl Friedrich Burdach (1800), and both Gottfried Reinhold Treviranus and Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1802.

paragraphs.heading: From Aristotle to the microscope
paragraphs.text: The earliest roots of science, medicine among them, go back to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, around 3000 to 1200 BCE, and these shaped Greek natural philosophy. Aristotle added a great deal, studying the causes behind living things and the variety of life. His successor Theophrastus started the scientific study of plants. Biology began to move quickly when Anton van Leeuwenhoek greatly improved the microscope, and it was then that scholars found sperm cells, bacteria and a whole world of tiny life.

paragraphs.heading: Cells, names and evolution
paragraphs.text: In 1838 Schleiden and Schwann argued that the cell is the basic unit of organisms. Robert Remak and Rudolf Virchow then showed that cells come from other cells dividing, and by the 1860s most biologists accepted cell theory. Carl Linnaeus had published a basic system for classifying nature in 1735. Charles Darwin built a theory of evolution based on natural selection, and Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same conclusions on his own.

paragraphs.heading: Genes and DNA
paragraphs.text: Modern genetics began with Gregor Mendel's work in 1865, which set out the rules of inheritance. Its importance was only grasped in the early 20th century, when the modern synthesis joined Darwin's evolution with classical genetics. Later, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase ran experiments that pointed to DNA as the part of chromosomes that carries genes. In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick found DNA's double-helix shape, opening the era of molecular genetics, and in 1990 the Human Genome Project set out to map the human genome.
